units.translation: The letter T in M is written by a later hand over an erasure of another letter. In most copies it is ἄγναμπτον [unbent, inflexible], in a few, among them the Vossian, ἄγναπτον [unbent, inflexible], with γρ άκαμπον [variant: unbent] also noted in one. The metrical fault—for the middle syllable of the word must be short—is not yet clear how it should be corrected. The verb from which ἄγναμπτος [unbent, inflexible] is derived is written below at v. 995 as γνάψει [will card] in M, with the letter μ written above by a corrector, by which γνάμψει [will bend] is indicated, which passed into many copies, just as in Persians v. 576 γναπτόμενοι [being carded], which the corrector left untouched in the codex, is written γναμπτόμενοι [being bent] in some later copies. Again, in Sophocles Ajax 1031 ἐκνάπτετο [was being carded], which the Laurentian codex had from the first hand, a later hand changed to ἐγνάπτετο [was being carded], received into most copies, except that in some it is ἐγνάμπτετο [was being bent]. For scribes have left the verb κνάπτω [to card] and its derivatives hardly anywhere untouched, but accustomed to Homeric γνάμπτειν [to bend] they have mostly written either thus or γνάπτειν [to card]: on which more has been said in the Thesaurus under γνάμπτω [to bend] and κνάπτω [to card]. Wherefore it is likely that in Aeschylus' verse too ἄγναμπτον [unbent, inflexible] was introduced for a cognate form having a short middle syllable, such as ἄκναφον [uncarded], differing in form only from ἄκναπτος [uncarded], which is said not only of garments that have not undergone fulling, but also improperly, as has been shown in the Thesaurus under ἄκναπτος [uncarded]: whence Hesychius explains it by ἀκατάκλαστος [unbending], in whose codex what is read, ἀκάαπτον (ἄκναπτον Musurus): ἀκατάκλαστον. ἄγναφον ἱμάτιον, καὶ ἀκόλαστον (ἄκλαστον Pierson), in whatever way it is arranged, it is clear that a double meaning has been noted by him, one proper, ἄγναφον ἱμάτιον [uncarded garment], the other improper ἀκατάκλαστος [unbending], which adjective Hesychius also uses under ἄκαμπτος [unbent], ἄκαμπτος (thus rightly H. Stephanus for άκαμπος): ἀκατάκλαστος, ἀκαμπής [unbending, inflexible], and schol. Hom. Od. 10, 329 σοὶ δέ τις ἐν στήθεσσιν ἀκήλητος νόος ἐστίν [but in your breast there is an unbeguiled mind], which he explains as άθελκτος, ἀκάκωτος, ἀκατάκλαστος [unbewitched, unharmed, unbending]. Further in Hesychius ἄκανθον: ἄγναμπτον (which Schmidt conjectured to have degenerated from ἄκναφον: ἄγναπτον) and ἀκάκαστον: ἀκαμπές [unbent]. τάν θεῶν ἄκαμπτον φρένα [the unbending mind of the gods] Euripides said Hippol. 1268, which I think Aeschylus would also have said, unless he had needed a word of cretic measure. ἄγναμπτον ἔχει νόον [he has an unbending mind] said Paulus Silentiarius Anthol. Planud. 4, 278. No less apt would be ἀστραφῆ νόον [unturning mind], which Hermann conjectured, trusting Hesychius, who however did not cite it from Aeschylus, but from Sophocles, ἀστραφής: σκληρός. Σοφοκλῆς Μυσοῖς [unbending: hard. Sophocles in the Mysians], ἀστραφές: ἄστρεπτον, ἀσφαλές [unturning: unturned, secure]. which second gloss is perhaps a dittography of the earlier gloss ἀστραβές: ἄστρεπτον καὶ ἀσφαλές [unturning: unturned and secure]. But if the old glossator had read ἀστραφῆ [unturning], he would have interpreted it by ἄστρεπτον [unturned] or ἄτρεπτον [unchangeable] rather than by ἄγναμπτον [unbent], or, if he had wanted to say inflexible, by ἄκαμπτον [unbent] rather than by ἄγναμπτον [unbent]. These things about this passage I wrote in the Preface to the London edition of Prometheus (1866) p. XI.
